introduction: This foundational level explores the chemistry of life and human application. It covers Biomolecules (the organic compounds that build and sustain living organisms), Polymers (macromolecules formed by repeating units), and Chemistry in Everyday Life (drugs, medicines, and cleansing agents).

core_concepts.title: Biomolecules: Carbohydrates
core_concepts.description:
Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. 
1. Monosaccharides: Simplest units that cannot be hydrolyzed further (e.g., Glucose, Fructose, Galactose). General formula: $(CH_2O)_n$.
2. Oligosaccharides: Yield 2-10 monosaccharide units upon hydrolysis (e.g., Sucrose, Lactose, Maltose).
3. Polysaccharides: Yield a large number of monosaccharides (e.g., Starch, Cellulose, Glycogen).

core_concepts.title: Biomolecules: Proteins and Amino Acids
core_concepts.description:
Proteins are unbranched polymers of $\alpha$-amino acids. 
Amino Acids contain both an amino group ($-NH_2$) and a carboxyl group ($-COOH$). Essential amino acids (e.g., Valine, Leucine) cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained through diet. Non-essential amino acids (e.g., Glycine, Alanine) can be synthesized in the body.

core_concepts.title: Polymers: Classification
core_concepts.description:
Polymers are high molecular mass macromolecules formed by repeating monomer units.
1. Natural Polymers: Found in plants and animals (e.g., Proteins, Cellulose, Starch, Natural Rubber).
2. Synthetic Polymers: Man-made (e.g., Plastics like Polythene, Synthetic fibers like Nylon-6,6).
3. Semi-synthetic Polymers: Cellulose derivatives (e.g., Cellulose acetate/Rayon).

core_concepts.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life: Drugs and Medicines
core_concepts.description:
Chemicals of low molecular masses interacting with macromolecular targets to produce a biological response.
- Analgesics: Reduce or abolish pain (e.g., Aspirin, Paracetamol). Aspirin also prevents platelet coagulation (prevents heart attacks).
- Antipyretics: Bring down body temperature in high fever (e.g., Paracetamol).
- Antacids: Neutralize excess stomach acid (e.g., $NaHCO_3$, $Mg(OH)_2$, Ranitidine/Zantac).

important_entities.name: Zwitterion (Dipolar Ion)
important_entities.key_fact: Amino acids exist as neutral but dual-charged species in aqueous solution.
important_entities.significance: In an aqueous solution, the carboxyl group loses a proton and the amino group accepts it, forming a species with both positive ($-NH_3^+$) and negative ($-COO^-$) charges. This is why amino acids exhibit amphoteric behavior and have high melting points (acting like salts rather than simple amines or acids).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: All monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) and most disaccharides (maltose, lactose) are 'Reducing Sugars' because they can reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents. Sucrose is a massive EXCEPTION. In sucrose, the reducing functional groups (the aldehyde group of glucose and the ketone group of fructose) are bonded to EACH OTHER via a glycosidic linkage. Since no free carbonyl group is available, Sucrose is a strictly NON-REDUCING sugar.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To remember vitamin solubility:
- Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K. They are stored in liver and adipose tissues.
- Water-soluble vitamins are B and C. They must be supplied regularly in the diet because they are readily excreted in urine (except Vitamin B12, which is stored in the liver).

exam_strategy_tips: Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic acid) is a highly tested molecule. Remember it acts as an Analgesic, an Antipyretic, AND an Anti-inflammatory drug. It is completely contraindicated for patients with ulcers because it hydrolyzes in the stomach to yield salicylic acid, causing severe bleeding.
